core.text: The fourth principal part, turned into an -us -a -um adjective, is **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudātus = praised)**: *puer laudātus* — the praised boy, the boy who has been praised. It describes a noun by something already done to it, and agrees with that noun like any adjective: *fīlum factum*, *catēna rupta*, *virī territī*. Latin name: *participium perfectī passīvī*.
A participle is a verb used like an adjective. English has one just like this: *a broken cup*, *a written letter* — *broken* and *written* describe the noun by what happened to it.
Participle stem + -us, -a, -um; declined like bonus. Meaning: 'having been …-ed'.

invented.en: The boy praised by the teacher is glad.

core.text: The same word with *est* becomes a whole verb, **the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudātus est)**: *puer laudātus est* — the boy was praised. Without *est* it just describes: *puer laudātus gaudet* — the praised boy is glad.

teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence says what was done to the water, and to the slaves?

teach.say: Take a verb and use it to describe a noun, and you have **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudātus = praised)**. It says what has been done to somebody: *puer laudātus*, the boy who has been praised. It is one word, and it describes its noun exactly as *bonus* or *magnus* would.

check.ask: Which word says what was done to the girl?

teach.title: Where it comes from, and its first three endings
teach.say: Take the fourth dictionary form, *laudātum*, cut the *-um*, and put on the endings of *bonus*: *laudātus* for a man, *laudāta* for a woman, *laudātum* for a thing. Nothing else changes. So *clausum ōstium* is a shut door and *portāta aqua* is water that has been carried.

check.ask: Fill in the three subject forms of the singular.

teach.title: It follows its noun into the object form
teach.say: Because it is an adjective it goes wherever its noun goes. When the noun is the object, the participle takes the object ending too: *epistulam scrīptam*, the written letter; *portam apertam*, the opened gate. The verb of the sentence never touches it.

check.ask: Fill in the two object forms of the singular.

teach.title: More than one
teach.say: In the plural, the endings of *bonus* again: *vocātī servī*, men who have been called; *carptae rosae*, roses that have been picked; *dicta verba*, words that have been spoken. Watch that last one: *dicta* is neuter plural here, not a feminine singular.

check.ask: Fill in the three subject forms of the plural.

teach.title: Done to him, or done by him?
teach.say: Latin has a second participle, **the present participle (the '-ing' word that describes a noun)**, and once you know the signal the two never blur. *-ns* means he is doing it; *-tus* or *-sus* means it was done to him. *puer vocātus* was called; *puer vocāns* is calling.

check.ask: *perterritī* — did the boys frighten, or were they frightened?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: In a real sentence the participle need not stand beside its noun, and it may come first: *in sacculō occultātam pecūniam*. Find the participle's ending, then find the noun carrying the same case, number and gender, and the pair falls out of the sentence by itself.

check.ask: *legō, legere, lēgī, lēctum*. Make the participle agree with *librum*.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 21) pair Latin's two true participles: present active in -ns (*ferēns* — carrying) and perfect passive in -tus (*lātus* — carried). There is no present passive or perfect active participle for ordinary verbs; a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) fills the second gap (*locūtus* — having spoken).

Endings vary: -tus (*laudātus, audītus, scrīptus*), -sus after certain consonants (*vīsus, missus, clausus, pulsus*). Many have become plain adjectives or nouns: *parātus* (ready), *factum* (a deed), *dictum* (a saying).
The one exception is a deponent — *locūtus* means he spoke; that comes next chapter.
